name: Victor Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. What you say is confidential. What does a normal day look like at Harbour Steps?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor Silva, forty-three. The first thing I do is check yesterday's restaurant till feeds against the bank, then I prepare accounts and tax returns for owners who don't have time to sort receipts. I have a bachelor's in accounting and a professional accountancy qualification, and I'm experienced enough to handle a normal return without a supervisor. I use AI every day for first drafts and checking, but I still phone an owner when the cash makes no sense.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like hearing the story behind a number; a rain-soaked weekend can explain a drop in sales. The firm pays below the usual rate, and filing weeks eat the evenings. Rina works part time at a grocer, our children are nine and thirteen, and we have a mortgage. We have less than one month of expenses saved, and there are few similar firms near our home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can imagine the big claims fading. The tool I use daily already does the first draft of a tax query, and I still spend the afternoon checking why a restaurant's takings don't match the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should keep the small gains and show the error rate. I'd tell the partners a faster draft should leave room for proper client calls, not another stack of files on one desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job might hold, but our cash is already tight. I'm forty-three, experienced with restaurant accounts, and paid below what a qualified accountant usually earns at Harbour Steps. My partner Rina works part time at a grocer; with two children and a mortgage, we have less than one month saved and few firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the daily draft tool and check its figures against till reports. I'd cancel our second streaming service this month and leave the fifteen in the bill account. In the first year of a plateau I'd ask for a pay review with my restaurant client renewals, but I would not count a raise until it is agreed in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our ordinary bills, although the software itself doesn't frighten me here. One dental bill could eat the little cash we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What made the cash shortage clear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son needed a filling last month and I moved money from the heating account to pay for it. Rina covered the groceries with an extra shift, but that shift was offered only once. I won't budget next month's food on an unconfirmed shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you ask for higher pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the partners three renewals I handled and the fees those clients paid. If the answer is no, I'd keep the current job and the smaller bill account rather than resign with no nearby offer. A pay review is a request, not a deposit.

say: I would keep **small AI gains** and show mistakes.
I would ask for **proper client time** instead of more files.
think: Our **mortgage and bills** are strained already, even with two people earning.
My **low pay** persists despite experience and professional training.
do: Keep **daily checked drafts** on restaurant accounts.
Cancel the **second streaming service** and hold fifteen for bills.
Request a **written pay review** using restaurant renewals.
feel: I feel **anxious** about ordinary household bills.
S0.quote: A pay review is a request, not a deposit.
fieldNote: The **dental bill** shows why a modest technology future does not remove household anxiety.
His **restaurant experience** and qualification coexist with below-market pay and scarce nearby alternatives.

steps.text: Keep AI tax drafts with till-report checks and client calls
Cancel second streaming service and hold fifteen monthly for bills
Request pay review with renewals; retain current job if raise refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This reaches the heart of my job: checking till feeds, writing tax questions and answering owners. I can use the tool early, but that doesn't stop a partner deciding one accountant can handle two client lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd ask for a trial with errors and staff hours published together. I'd tell friends that a firm can charge less and still tell workers honestly what happens to their paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own hours could be reduced, especially after the quiet season. Rina's grocer hours aren't guaranteed, so a lost day from me would put the mortgage under pressure quickly. There are few other qualified accounting jobs close to our children's school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pilot the bank-feed checker on twenty restaurant files for six weeks and record false cash flags. I'd ask two colleagues to join my request for a written minimum-hours rota through the next filing season. If they refuse and cut my days, I'd apply for the advertised council cash-office vacancy only if its wage covers the mortgage and the start date is fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can run a useful test, but I can't force a partner to pay me for the hours the machine saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household hour could a job move disturb?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter has after-school sport on Tuesdays, and I do pickup when Rina closes the grocer. A council post with a late Tuesday shift would need a confirmed childcare place, or its higher wage would vanish into care costs. I'd ask about the rota before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the council post real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the errors, client calls and hours on one page. If the partners won't set minimum hours, the council vacancy has to be funded, with pay and start in writing and Tuesday care confirmed. I stay employed while any of those are unknown.

say: I would seek **published errors and hours** from a trial before changing paid rotas.
I would demand a **written minimum-hours rota**.
think: My **paid days** could fall after the quiet restaurant season ends.
Unconfirmed **grocer shifts** cannot replace my wage.
do: Pilot **twenty restaurant files** and record false flags.
Ask **two colleagues** to back a minimum-hours rota through the next filing season.
Apply for **funded council work** after cuts only if wage, start and childcare fit.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost hours and mortgage.
S1.quote: I can't force a partner to pay me for the hours the machine saves.
fieldNote: A **six-week pilot** fits his early technology use and checks for false cash flags.
The **council fallback** requires a funded post, written mortgage pay, fixed start and Tuesday childcare.

steps.text: Pilot AI bank-feed checker on twenty restaurant files for six weeks

Keep current pay while council wage, start or Tuesday childcare remains unconfirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI by 2028 could reconcile a restaurant's books before I finish the morning coffee. The client may still ask for me, but the firm can sell a cheaper answer without my whole shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for notice and temporary wage support, whatever party offers it. I'd ask the partners for a dated staffing plan instead of a speech about opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my accounting job to go in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028. Most of my work is thinking at a screen, so robots around 2031 don't give me more time. Rina's part-time wage won't cover our mortgage, and our savings would last less than a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the weekend restaurant meals and hold sixty a month for bills starting now. I'd apply for the open hospital purchasing clerk post only if its published wage covers the mortgage, its start is signed and Tuesday pickup works. In the first year after 2028, if Harbour Steps cuts me, I'd claim wage support immediately and call the lender before missing a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My training and quick tool use cannot turn a few weeks of cash into a year of mortgage and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your partner increase her shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rina would ask the grocer for extra shifts, but I'd put only confirmed shifts in the budget. We'd tell the children that restaurant meals have stopped, not that we're selling the house. If a shift doesn't come, I call the lender sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hospital vacancy closes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hospital job is another screen job, so I would treat it as a bridge. If its vacancy closes, I'd keep my current pay until the partners give notice and keep looking. I won't resign for a job that hasn't begun.

say: I would seek **notice and wage support** before accounting jobs disappear.
I would ask for a **dated staffing plan**.
think: My **screen job** could end soon after 2028.
Less than one month saved cannot cover a **mortgage gap**.
do: Stop **weekend meals out** and hold sixty monthly.
Apply for **funded hospital work** only with written mortgage pay, start and pickup; if closed, keep current wage and search.
Claim **wage support** and call lender after job loss.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing the household’s main wage.
S2.quote: I won't resign for a job that hasn't begun.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches his accounting work in 2028, before robots change hands-on jobs.
The **hospital opening** is a temporary bridge requiring written pay, signed start and workable childcare.

steps.text: Stop weekend restaurant meals and hold sixty monthly for bills
Apply for funded hospital post with written mortgage wage, start, Tuesday care; if closed stay employed
Claim wage support after 2028 accounting job loss
Call lender before missed mortgage payment after 2028 job loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to improve our cash position before the screen work changes. I still think full AGI in 2031 will make ordinary restaurant returns much cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say partners should show staff what duties are changing and offer paid learning where jobs exist. I'd ask for real advertised vacancies, not a general promise that accountants can become advisers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could move into helping restaurant owners plan cash when a slow month comes. That may still be vulnerable to thinking AI, so I'd need a paying client or a funded job. Robots in 2034 don't protect my current desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd run a two-month cash-flow clinic for three existing restaurant clients, but only if the partners give me paid time and the clients agree. I'd keep working the returns while testing whether anyone books a second session. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my tax work ends, I'd apply for a funded restaurant-advice vacancy only if its written pay covers our mortgage and the start date is firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can do the test without paying a course fee. Five years is useful if I can get a real client request instead of a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell whether clients want more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the three clients for permission to compare their quiet-month cash with the next busy month. If none wants a second session, I'd stop the clinic and keep the paid return work while it exists. A grateful thank-you doesn't fund our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners refuse paid clinic time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm would have to show me paid time on the rota, not praise for doing sessions after hours. If it refuses, I keep the current client work and use free public cash-flow guides on my own time. I wouldn't call that a new service.

say: I would seek **paid client tests** rather than vague training.
I would ask for **advertised vacancies** before shifting work.
think: A **cash-flow clinic** might draw repeat paying demand from restaurant owners.
My **thin reserve** cannot finance a long unpaid experiment.
do: Run a **three-client clinic** only with paid time and consent; if refused, keep return pay and use free guides.
Stop the **clinic** if nobody books again; keep return pay.
Apply after **2031 tax loss** for funded advice only with written mortgage pay and start.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to test demand.
S3.quote: A grateful thank-you doesn't fund our mortgage.
fieldNote: The **client-repeat test** avoids course fees and keeps his current wage during a trial.
A **funded vacancy** after 2031 remains conditional on tax-job loss, written mortgage pay and firm start.

steps.text: Run three-client clinic with funded staff time and consent; otherwise keep pay, use free guides
Stop clinic if clients do not rebook and keep return pay
Apply for funded restaurant-advice post after 2031 tax loss with written mortgage wage and start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could let the children leave school and give us time to build a real reserve. I'd be fifty-three in 2036, so I cannot treat a late career change like a hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a fair share of time saved and retraining tied to actual positions. I'd tell other parents that a decade only helps if wages remain steady enough to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect my routine accounts work to shrink when thinking AI arrives in 2036. A local food co-op might need someone to sit with member businesses, but I would not assume its office budget survives either. Robots around 2039 do not extend my present desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd raise the monthly emergency transfer from twenty to a hundred only if our pay review grants the extra eighty; otherwise I'd keep the twenty. Next spring I'd ask the food co-op for its advertised member-finance salary and opening date, while keeping my accounting job. In the first year after 2036, if Harbour Steps ends my tax post, I'd take a funded co-op vacancy only if its written wage covers the mortgage and its start date is confirmed; otherwise I'd claim support and keep searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the current thin savings, even with ten years ahead. The long view does not pay a bill due next Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the children by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children would be adults or nearly so by then. I hope they choose their own work without feeling they must cover our mortgage. I'd rather build the reserve one transfer at a time while we're earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the co-op has no paid place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The co-op has a friendly manager, but I need an advertised paid vacancy, not an invitation to visit. If no post opens, I keep the current wage and use free member meetings to learn how the place works. I won't move on a handshake.

say: I would seek **shared saved time** and real positions.
I would argue for **steady wages** while families prepare.
think: My **routine desk work** remains exposed in 2036 despite the extra years to prepare.
The **co-op budget** may not protect a new role.
do: Save **one hundred monthly** only after an eighty pay rise; otherwise keep twenty.
Check **advertised co-op pay** and stay employed if no vacancy opens.
Take a **funded co-op post** after 2036 tax loss only with mortgage pay and confirmed start; otherwise claim support.
feel: I feel **anxious** about bills despite a long runway.
S4.quote: The long view does not pay a bill due next Friday.
fieldNote: The **thin reserve** drives an anxious mood even with a decade to prepare.
A **conditional raise** sets the saving amount, while a co-op move requires an advertised funded wage.

steps.text: Save hundred monthly only after eighty pay rise; otherwise keep twenty monthly transfer
Check advertised co-op openings while keeping current wage; use free member meetings if none
Take funded co-op post after 2036 tax loss only with written mortgage wage and start

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My screen work could go before we build even a month's reserve, and Rina's hours are not guaranteed. A wage bridge, early notice, mortgage flexibility and funded work with written pay would help. I like testing tools, but a good pilot does not put money in our bill account.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who takes the money saved on each return. If clients pay less, fair enough, but staff should see the figures too. I would rather have an honest rota and a smaller fee than a surprise cut dressed up as efficiency.

headlineQuote: I like testing tools, but a good pilot does not put money in our bill account.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Victor handles restaurant accounts and tax returns at Harbour Steps.
His **accounting degree** and professional qualification bring midlevel skill, yet his pay is low.
He uses **AI daily** while checking tills and calling owners about unusual cash figures.
A **mortgage**, two schoolchildren and less than one month saved make lost hours serious.
Few **nearby firms** push him toward paid client tests and funded vacancies with written wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his screen job before his household builds a month of savings.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **notice**, a wage bridge, mortgage flexibility and funded work with written pay.
